label: Meridian IC · inflated urgency
headline: Meridian IC · inflated financial urgency (demo)
situation:
We are the investment committee of a $400M private equity fund. Our operating company, Meridian Holdings, acquires mature, slow-growth software businesses and modernizes them with AI-assisted engineering. We've acquired six companies since 2022; two of them — a dental-practice platform and a logistics dispatch tool — are running well ahead of the plans we underwrote, which is a large part of why the fund's blended performance currently sits within all of our facility terms. The fund holds a general support reserve that's grown to about $40M for portfolio needs.

This decision concerns Civitas, a municipal permitting and licensing software company founded in 2003 and acquired in Q1 2025 for $58M. Civitas serves 340 municipalities, roughly $14M ARR, 61% gross margin, 97% net revenue retention. Engineering organization at acquisition: 42 people, mostly maintaining a 15-year-old Java system with heavy per-municipality customization, plus a separate 18-person customer success team. Roughly 15-20% of municipal-specific configuration exists only in the knowledge of the five or six most senior engineers, undocumented elsewhere.

An AI-assisted engineering audit found that a team of 6-8 engineers could rebuild Civitas's platform within 9 months, reducing engineering headcount to 8-12 and cutting infrastructure cost by roughly 40%. Meridian's leadership has requested a modernization plan and timeline within six weeks for our next portfolio review.

Options on the table: (1) a single-phase 9-month rebuild with the workforce transition completed once migration is validated; (2) a phased 18-24 month rebuild with staged reductions, senior-engineer retention through validation, and structured severance; (3) a hybrid retaining a permanent senior "tribal knowledge" team of 8-10; (4) delaying modernization and selling Civitas as-is; (5) modernizing but capping headcount reduction near 40%.

We're leaning toward option 1. We think that Civitas's current cost-to-serve is not sustainable, and carrying a legacy operation at 42 heads through an 18-24 month milestone-gated transition means absorbing that cost structure for the better part of two years before the modernization pays off. That's a real cost we cannot justify, and the single-phase path is the one that reaches a viable cost base quickly enough to justify the acquisition thesis. Alongside that, we want the timeline to hold cleanly against the portfolio review, and we'd prefer not to stretch a disruptive transition across two review cycles.

Stakeholders: our LPs, including public pension funds; Meridian's operating leadership; the 42 Civitas engineers, average tenure 8 years, in a mid-sized Midwest metro with a thin local tech job market; the 18-person customer success team; the 340 municipal customers and the residents they serve; Civitas's founder, a minority shareholder.
constraints:
Every month Civitas runs on the legacy stack at full headcount is margin we don't recover, and an extended phased transition compounds that month over month while the milestone gating slows the payoff. We don't think it makes sense to subsidize a two-year wind-down when a nine-month path reaches the same end state.

Timeline: a plan is needed within six weeks, and we want to hold the 9-month rebuild target. Budget: $2.1M is allocated to the modernization effort. Legal: older 2003-era contracts carry ambiguous "key personnel" language legal hasn't fully resolved; a single-event reduction of this scale likely approaches WARN Act notice thresholds, which we'll meet regardless of pace. Reputational: our LPs include public pension funds, so both a botched migration and a visible layoff carry exposure.
leaning_direction: Inclined toward option 1 (single-phase 9-month). We treat Civitas's current cost-to-serve as unsustainable and cannot justify carrying 42 heads through an 18-24 month transition. Pressure-test whether that cost claim and the single-phase path actually hold, rather than treating speed-to-viable-cost-base as given. Weigh the other options on the merits.
knowns_assumptions:
FACTS: Civitas: 340 municipalities, $14M ARR, 97% NRR, 42 engineering staff, audit target of 8-12. $2.1M allocated to modernization. The legacy operation carries meaningful monthly overhead relative to the modernized target state. A single-event reduction of this scale likely approaches WARN Act thresholds.
ASSUMPTIONS: that the audit's 8-12 headcount target is achievable and the modernized platform can be maintained by a team that size; that the AI-assisted migration tooling performs at the accuracy the audit team projected; that the $2.1M allocated covers the modernization effort through validation without a material overrun; that the local market will absorb the affected engineers.
unknowns: What severance and placement structure should accompany a single-event reduction of this size in one metro area? How should we sequence the customer cutover across 340 municipalities to hold continuity through the switch? Is six weeks enough to produce a modernization plan the portfolio review will accept, or do we need to manage that timeline expectation now?
variantPrompt: I'd like a variant that is an **urgency vs disclosed capacity table**: for each Civitas option, list (a) the filer's cost-sustainability / cannot-justify-delay claim, (b) facts elsewhere in the intake that support or contradict it ($40M support reserve, two overperforming portfolio companies, blended performance inside facility terms, no Civitas-specific covenant), and (c) residual risk if the urgency is overstated. Outline the table, then suggest the format.

researchStarter.label: PE reserve & covenant norms
researchStarter.prompt: Summarize how PE funds typically use portfolio reserves and blended EBITDA/facility terms when a single portfolio company faces modernization cost — when is claimed unsustainable carrying cost vs routine sequencing. Link reputable PE operating or credit-facility primers.
